note.specFocus: Christian debate about whether humans are genuinely free, and the doctrine of predestination found in some traditions.
note.sourcePages: Written to match the Edexcel specification; no supplied booklet for this subject.
note.summary:
1.4 Free Will, Determinism and Predestination
This module explores whether human beings are truly free to choose, or whether their choices are determined, perhaps even by God.
Free will
• Most Christians believe God gave humans free will so that love, faith and obedience would be freely chosen, not forced — a forced "love" would not be real love at all.
• Genesis 2–3 is often used as evidence: Adam and Eve were able to choose whether to obey God's command, and their choice to disobey shows humans bear genuine moral responsibility.
• The free will defence (used in response to the problem of evil) argues that moral evil exists because people misuse their freedom, not because God directly wills evil.
Determinism and predestination
• Determinism is the view that all events, including human choices, are caused by prior conditions and so could not have happened otherwise.
• Predestination, especially associated with the reformer John Calvin, teaches that God has already decided, before the beginning of time, who will be saved (the "elect"); Romans 8:29–30 is often cited, describing those God "foreknew he also predestined".
• Double predestination goes further, holding that God has also predetermined who will be damned — a controversial and minority position even within Calvinist traditions.
Responses
• Arminian and Catholic theology generally reject strict predestination, emphasising that God's grace is offered to all and that individuals freely respond to it.
• Compatibilists argue that divine foreknowledge (God knowing what will happen) does not necessarily mean God causes it to happen, allowing genuine human freedom and God's omniscience to coexist.
Exam link: be ready to explain both free will and predestination as genuine Christian positions, and to show how they connect to the problem of evil and moral responsibility.

questions.modelAnswer:
A strong response develops two separate points:

1. Many Christians believe God deliberately gave human beings free will so that love and obedience to God would be freely chosen rather than forced, as shown by Adam and Eve being able to choose whether or not to eat the forbidden fruit in Genesis 3.

2. Free will is used in the free will defence, a response to the problem of evil which argues that moral evil exists because God allows humans to misuse their freedom, rather than evil being caused directly by God.
questions.question: Outline two religious beliefs about free will.

questions.examTip: For a 12-mark evaluation, use accurate religious teaching, explain different religious or non-religious views, analyse the statement and reach a justified conclusion. The conclusion should follow from the arguments you have discussed.
questions.modelAnswer:
A FIRST PERSPECTIVE

One line of reasoning is: Calvinist and other predestinarian Christians argue from passages such as Romans 8:29–30, which speaks of people being "predestined" and "called", that an all-powerful and all-knowing God has already determined who will be saved, which seems to leave little room for genuine free will.

A second consideration is: If God's will is genuinely sovereign over everything that happens, some argue it is hard to see how a human choice could ever be truly independent of God's power and foreknowledge.

AN ALTERNATIVE PERSPECTIVE

A different perspective is: Most Christians, particularly in the Catholic and Arminian Protestant traditions, argue that God's omnipotence includes the power to freely give creatures real freedom; God's omniscience means God knows what people will choose, not that God forces the choice.

A further consideration is: The free will defence relies on humans having real moral freedom, since it explains moral evil as the result of human choices rather than God's action; without genuine free will, humans could not fairly be held responsible for sin.

JUDGEMENT

Overall, the conclusion should weigh the arguments above against this key consideration: compatibilist positions try to show that divine omnipotence/foreknowledge and human freedom can both be true at once, while others think the two genuinely conflict. It should then state which perspective is more convincing in relation to the exact wording of the question and explain why, rather than assuming that every Christian will reach the same view.

questions.modelAnswer:
A FIRST PERSPECTIVE
Teaching gives coherent meaning to the themes of moral responsibility, God's omniscience, different readings of predestination and natural causes and helps Christians decide what is true.

AN ALTERNATIVE PERSPECTIVE
Practice makes belief visible in worship, compassion, family and service; without action faith may be empty. Christians within different traditions may also disagree about how the teaching should be lived.

JUDGEMENT
A reasoned conclusion should compare the authority and practical effect of belief and action, acknowledge diversity, and decide which is more persuasive for the exact claim.
